#4295. Capcom Reveals Fanmade Robot Master for Mega Man: Dual Override

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

The most iconic characters in the Mega Man franchise, second only to ol’ Rock himself, are the Robot Masters, the powerful, highly-specialized robots built by Dr. Light, Dr. Wily, or whoever else who are programmed to wreak havoc upon the world, usually in batches of eight. Naturally, the newest upcoming entry in the mainline series, Mega Man: Dual Override, will have a new swath of Robot Masters to do battle with, several of which like Jet Man, Cook Man, and Twinkle Girl have already been revealed.

However, in addition to these new Capcom-made Robot Masters, Dual Override is slated to bring back a long-dormant tradition of the Mega Man series: fan-designed Robot Masters. Not long after the game’s initial reveal, Capcom launched a character design contest in which fans were encouraged to design their own original Robot Master and submit it for a chance to be included in the game.

Capcom showed off a new Mega Man: Dual Override demo at Tokyo Game Show this year, proving the veteran franchise has still got it.

Many months later, Capcom has officially announced the winner of this contest and revealed the fanmade Robot Master who will be joining the rest of the new Wily Numbers. Strap on your scouring pads and turn your spray nozzles to “ON,” because our latest menace is Cleanser Man.

As director Shinya Ikuta and producer Hiroyuki Minamitani announced in a video revealed during its TwitchCon 2026 panel and posted to the official Mega Man YouTube channel, Cleanser Man was selected out of around 10,000 entrants into the contest from around the world, which then had to be meticulously narrowed down to 20 proper participants, followed by just 6 finalists. These 6 finalists included Sweeper Woman, Recycle Man, Juggle Man, Valve Man, Cactus Man, and of course, Cleanser Man.

“In the end, we chose Cleanser Man because of the unique way the concept was brought together and the originality of the color design,” Ikuta explained.

These 6 finalists included Sweeper Woman, Recycle Man, Juggle Man, Valve Man, Cactus Man, and of course, Cleanser Man.

According to an official character summary sent by Capcom to Game Informer, Cleanser Man is a cleaning robot with an obsessive love of all things sparkling and pristine who will go to absurd lengths to scrub out any perceived imperfections, even if he ends up breaking things in the process. His stage will be set in a trash processing plant that’s flooding the world with garbage so people better appreciate his dedication to cleanliness.

The Tokyo Game Show 2026 Presentation revealed new details regarding both the second protagonist and the game's core mechanics.

Cleanser Man comes to us from a Brazilian artist who goes by “miya” on their X, formerly Twitter account. Upon the reveal that their design was chosen, they posted a screencap of Cleanser Man’s official render side-by-side with their concept art, adding the caption, “The attention to detail almost made me cry. It truly means a lot.”

Not only was the character-design contest a fun way to get people hyped up for Mega Man: Dual Override, not to mention showcase some really cool character-design work, it’s also an important revival of a long-forgotten Mega Man tradition.

Following the release of the original Mega Man game and prior to the release of Mega Man 2, Capcom held a similar contest for its Japanese players to decide the designs of that game’s eight Robot Master. This contest format would be repeated for every subsequent mainline Mega Man game up to and including Mega Man 8, resulting in many of the most notoriously-difficult Robot Masters, before being discontinued from Mega Man & Bass through Mega Man 11. While there was still some fan design encouragement, it was mostly relegated to spin-off series like Battle Network and Star Force.

While it’s only for a single Robot Master rather than a full set of eight, Cleanser Man is still the first fanmade Robot Master to make it into a mainline Mega Man title since 1996, with the added accolade that he’s the first Robot Master to come from a designer in South America. It’ll truly be an honor to shove my Buster Gun in his face.

Mega Man has had a storied career, featured in many iconic games. This list breaks down the best Mega Man games out there.

#4293. Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.

Researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease. In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.

The results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the new findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," said Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.

How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk

To investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.

Participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.

This distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.

People consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.

Moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.

Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.

Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks

The clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.

These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.

However, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.

People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.

The contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.

By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

These percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.

"Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen said. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk."

Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?

Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.

Red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.

These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.

Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.

Wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.

Beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.

Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.

"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen said.

What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health

To make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.

Cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several important limitations.

Because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.

Alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.

Another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.

The researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.

Nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.

The findings highlight an important distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.

For now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.

Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

Materials provided by American College of Cardiology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4292. 2027 Scion Kei-01 First Drive: Mite Makes Right

We spent a little bit of time driving a short distance in a tiny pickup that’ll be sold in small numbers.

We haven’t timed one, but eyeballing it, the Scion Kei-01 should reach its top speed before the 1250-hp Chevy Corvette ZR1X reaches 100 mph. (You’re welcome, Toyota marketing team.) Of course, that’s because America’s newest and cutest truck is limited to just 25 mph, per the feds’ FMVSS No. 500 regulation that allows the Kei-01 to be sold here. Toyota is assembling and selling these rebadged Daihatsu Hijets in the United States starting next year, and we got to take one for a short drive—which will be most drives in a pickup this small—to see whether it lives up to the hype.

First, we had to fight our instinct to get into the driver’s seat from the left side. The Kei-01 is right-hand drive, like the Hijet sold in Japan, because Toyota wanted to bring it to the United States as quickly and inexpensively as possible. Production models will get a different backup camera to meet federal requirements, but beyond that, the U.S. version is largely unchanged from the Daihatsu sold in Japan.

See all results for used cars for sale near 19106

Every Kei-01 sold here, mainly to fleets, will have an extended cab, which affords extra cargo space for a shotgun or your largest bushel of chewing tobacco. Or both. The fixed steering column doesn’t tilt or telescope, but stovepipe-hat enthusiasts—and it’s been a while since they’ve heard this—have reason to celebrate, as the one thing this truck does big is headroom.

The Kei-01’s “jumbo” cab is why it stands just 2.9 inches lower in height than an F-150, but it’s a lot easier to get into. You barely have to lift a foot to climb in. A portion of the footwell is painted metal, and your feet are ahead of the front wheel wells. The front axle is practically beneath your butt.

Unlike the workaday pickups you can rent from Home Depot and Menards, this truck, with its massive screen and power windows, is an ergonomic miracle compared with single-cab full-size rentals. Remember when steering wheels were only responsible for turning left and right and occasionally honking the horn? The Kei-01’s wheel is like that. Except the horn’s high-pitched beep is too humiliating to use in anger.

Your fingertips on the steering wheel are so close to the front of the vehicle that they could almost be the hood ornament. Which is certainly novel and makes it super easy to nose in close to objects. Though the lack of a crumple zone aft of your knuckles is a concern that flashes through your mind.

Around the little dirt loop, the Kei-01 offers a driving feel that’s akin to a riding lawn mower. The steering takes nearly 4.5 turns lock-to-lock, but the Kei-01 is still stupid-easy to maneuver. There’s a rawness about scooting around in it that makes you feel like you’re getting paid hourly. This workhorse may be at a speed disadvantage compared to most of the electric scooters in our Gear Team’s roundup, but try hauling hay with one of those.

See all results for used cars for sale near 19106

Underneath all that adorable sheetmetal is a 660-cc three-cylinder engine that sounds about as smooth as a Honda Grom. It’s paired with a continuously variable automatic transmission. Despite its goofy proportions, the Kei-01 isn’t as front-heavy as it looks. With the engine mounted near the middle of the truck, this little box on wheels feels balanced. It lacks a dedicated transfer case, but its four-wheel-drive system has an electronic lock mode to add a bit more confidence on hill climbs.

The best part might be the roughly five-and-a-half-foot bed. Its low load floor makes for a perfect bench, and all three bedsides fold down. Lower the tailgate, or either side, or all three. It’s brilliantly simple and quick. There’s no tall bedside to reach over, and you don’t have to climb into the bed to reach stuff. The truck can handle 600 pounds of cargo too. Seriously, why can’t full-size pickup beds offer this kind of flexibility?

We spent only a short time driving the little Kei-01, but even limited to 25 mph, it’s still rather compelling. And, unlike the used kei trucks imported from Japan, the Scion has a factory warranty. The big unknown still hanging over this small truck is the price, which Toyota hasn’t announced yet. When all you need is a little truck, without most of the drawbacks of a big one, the Kei-01 certainly fits.

Austin Irwin has worked for Car and Driver for over 10 years in various roles. He's steadily worked his way from an entry-level data entry position into driving vehicles for photography and video, and is now reviewing and testing cars. What will he do next? Who knows, but he better be fast.

#4290. 2026 Toyota GRMN Corolla First Drive: A Blur of Nür

Toyota’s most expensive Corolla ever bristles with track-focused hardware.

Slapping Turn 1’s bright-green curbing, it’s immediately clear that the GR team has done something really good. I’m driving the Toyota GRMN Corolla at Eagles Canyon Raceway in Texas, and the first 30 seconds of recorded voice notes are just me eagerly repeating “Aw, yeah” at various parts of the track.

The GRMN, which stands for “Gazoo Racing tuned by Meister of Nürburgring,” receives an incredible amount of attention for a car Toyota won’t build more than 730 of. The changes are as juicy as workplace gossip. Ten slots are cut into the underside of the carbon-fiber hood to direct air where Toyota says it will contribute to more predictable steering at high speeds. Engineers shortened the front suspension’s bump-stop stroke by four millimeters while adding two millimeters at the rear, helping the car settle over curbing. There’s also a taller first gear and a pinch more torque in the midrange. And finally, an optional oil cooler keeps the all-wheel-drive system happy.

See all results for new 2027 Toyota GR Corolla for sale near 48184

Toyota’s obsession over details is admirable. The GRMN’s improvements over the standard GR are so subtle that they may go unnoticed by most folks and even some car nerds. I started my track time with an automatic GR Corolla, then switched to the GRMN and back. While the car looks only slightly different, the driving experience is wildly new.

The steering is the first major giveaway. Immediately, the GRMN feels much tighter and more direct in turns than the regular GR Corolla. Turn-in is dramatically quicker, and return to center is noticeably stronger. Initially, I thought Toyota had maybe beefed up its steering-rack slider. Nope. It’s largely the same hardware, but with an aggressive electric power-steering calibration. Adding to the different steering feel is a thinner steering-wheel rim, because even if it saved GR engineers less than an ounce, it still counts.

But it’s the suspension that really shines here. Eagles Canyon is rife with elevation changes, including several corners with curbing that would upset the automatic GR and send it bouncing upon landing. But like a honey badger, the GRMN don’t care. There’s no ugly secondary motion; you certainly feel the curb, but the nose stays flat on impact. Toyota developed special monotube dampers with internal rebound springs to help maintain tire contact, while its bump-stop changes convince you corner exit speeds are higher than ever. It’s the most Porsche-like behavior I’ve experienced in any car that competes with a Hyundai Elantra.

It’s worth noting that the regular GR that I drove wore Michelin Pilot Sport 4S tires, while the GRMN was on much stickier Pilot Sport Cup 2s. Some of the additional grip and steering response is absolutely down to the rubber, but the way the suspension manages impacts and keeps the body under control is an improvement that can’t be credited to tires alone.

See all results for new 2027 Toyota GR Corolla for sale near 48184

There is one exception to the GRMN’s good times that not even GRMN chief engineer Naoyuki Sakamoto could explain. During quick countersteering inputs, the electric steering occasionally delivers an unnatural kick through the wheel. It feels as though the power assist has reached its limit, though just for a moment. We experienced it three times over at least 20 laps, but never during our street drive.

The GRMN uses that same ole G16E-GTS 300-hp turbocharged 1.6-liter three-cylinder. Torque increases by just seven pound-feet to 302, with Toyota concentrating the additional grunt between 4000 and 4600 rpm, where the engine spent much of its time at Eagles Canyon clawing out of corners.

The six-speed manual gets its own collection of changes. The close-ratio EA68F gearbox has a taller first gear and a shorter third gear, changing how the engine works through its powerband. Engineers even revised the shifter-cable mount to make the action more direct. Having driven a manual GR recently, the difference is obvious. It’s not Honda Civic Type R good, but it’s still really good.

The GRMN also has additional cooling hardware and a driver-actuated intercooler water-spray system. The only other car I’ve ever driven with one of these was the Subaru WRX STI S209, which would make for a rather interesting comparison test if Subaru still built it. A one-gallon water tank sits beneath the GRMN’s cargo floor, supplying enough water to spray the intercooler for approximately 150 seconds. Toyota claims this can lower intake temperatures by roughly 14 to 20 degrees Fahrenheit. Unfortunately, it’s somewhat difficult to see the status of the system, as there’s no indication in the gauge cluster. Instead, the small button has an even tinier amber light that blinks slowly while two nozzles spray water onto the intercooler. It’s no place to have your eyes pointed while setting lap times, and it left us prayin’ it was still sprayin’.

The most important update may be the optional oil cooler for the all-wheel-drive transfer unit. During Lightning Lap testing in regular GR Corollas at Virginia International Raceway, we’ve experienced overheating that triggers the dreaded “AWD System Overheated” warning. Toyota’s solution circulates gear oil through a separate heat exchanger using an electric pump, roughly doubling the system’s oil capacity in the process.

However, the cooler isn’t standard equipment, and installing it involves more than bolting on a few hoses. It requires an ECU reflash and activation procedure, as the system’s electrical demands also introduce a fuel-economy penalty. Toyota installed the accessory on our GRMN before we took it onto the circuit. Its own testing suggests the system will prevent the AWD system from ever entering 2WD mode. That’s promising, although even 20 laps at Eagles Canyon (with the front straight closed) aren’t enough to declare the problem solved. We’d love to see how it handles VIR’s 4.1-mile Grand Course.

Eventually, Toyota representatives politely suggested I take a break from lapping the GRMN, motioning toward the line of other journalists in the pits. Ugh, fine. Later, I got another turn behind the wheel for the drive from the track to the hotel. And what a completely different experience that was.

As in the GR Corolla Morizo Edition, Toyota has stripped the rear seats from this four-door hatchback as part of an effort to reduce weight by 66 pounds. The rear windows are fixed. There’s no rear wiper either, which Toyota says saves about two pounds.

The GRMN is incredibly loud on public roads. With the rear seats removed, there’s little separating the cabin from the racket coming from behind. Those Cup 2 tires scream over mixed asphalt, their noise changing pitch with every new section of pavement. On the highway, you find yourself yelling at the passenger next to you, and not because they started talking politics.

The ride is similarly uncompromising. The same suspension that so calmly devours curbing at Eagles Canyon can make ordinary pavement feel jarring. Even the steering, which I couldn’t stop praising on the circuit, takes some getting used to, as it’s so quick on the street, where small inputs produce immediate responses.

I guess that’s why they didn’t name it the Corolla GR Route 380.

The GRMN Corolla starts at $65,655, which is about $24K more than the standard car. That almost GR86-sized price gap is no small upcharge for a Corolla that’s heavy on track ability and light on everyday ability. It’s also interesting that of the 730 GRMN Corollas being built, none will be sold in Germany, home of the actual Nürburgring; it’s a Japan, Australia, and North America offering only.

At one point during the drive event, one of the GRMNs picked up a nail in its tire, and Toyota had to pull it from the drive rotation to give it fresh Michelins. Rather than sit around and pout (as journalists sometimes do), influencers and editors climbed into the regular automatic GR Corolla for a few laps. The lack of complaining during that inconvenience proves my next point.

The GRMN’s biggest rival is the regular GR Corolla. The new car’s tiny yet important improvements make it considerably better on track, but is a few tenths per lap worth $24K? Not to mention the street-driving inconveniences? Maybe, for some. For everyone else, there’s a perfectly good GR Corolla with rear seats that doesn’t require earplugs.

#4289. Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

As marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering important questions about its effects on mental health. A major new study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

"What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," said lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an important mental health concern that deserves attention."

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link

The connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults showed particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

The consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

Yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

"Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood."

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

The study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is important because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

The findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

"Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," said Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support."

The study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an important role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked."

See the 2027 Toyota GRMN Corolla from every angle.

More carbon, more wing, more carbon wing—the 2026 Toyota GRMN Corolla is the most aggressive (and expensive) Corolla yet. It has slightly more torque than the normal Corolla, but great efforts have gone into refining its steering, suspension, and cooling.

Only 730 GRMN Corollas will be built, and a few have already arrived to customers. The GRMN is available only in North America, Japan, and Australia.

The big carbon-fiber wing at the top of the hatch has five angles of adjustability. One thing you can’t change is which transmission it comes with. The GRMN is sold exclusively with a six-speed manual.

#4287. Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain

Popular medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, may have effects that extend beyond weight loss and blood sugar control. These drugs also influence biological processes involved in brain function, raising questions about whether they could help preserve memory and thinking abilities.

To examine this possibility, researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen reviewed the existing scientific evidence at the invitation of the journal Science.

Studies involving animals suggest that GLP-1 medications can influence learning and memory. However, research involving humans has produced less consistent findings. Analyses of patient health records have found an association between GLP-1 treatment and a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes. These observational findings are encouraging, but they cannot determine whether the medications themselves are responsible for the lower risk.

More definitive results have also raised questions. In Novo Nordisk's EVOKE and EVOKE+ clinical trials, semaglutide failed to slow the progression of early Alzheimer's disease. Although the treatment affected several biological markers associated with Alzheimer's, those changes did not translate into a measurable slowing of the disease.

Why Weight Loss Drugs May Still Benefit the Brain

Despite the disappointing Alzheimer's results, researchers believe GLP-1 medications could still offer cognitive benefits to certain groups of patients.

People living with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience difficulties with attention, planning, and the speed at which they process information. These cognitive problems are often associated with metabolic health and blood vessel function, suggesting they may respond differently to treatment than the changes caused by Alzheimer's disease.

Improving blood sugar regulation, metabolism, or vascular health could potentially help preserve cognitive abilities, even if the same medications cannot slow an established neurodegenerative disease.

Stina Börchers, the review's first author and a researcher affiliated with both the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen, emphasizes the need to determine whether starting treatment earlier could make a difference.

"We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit," says Stina Börchers.

Unlocking New Treatments to Protect Memory

A central unanswered question is how GLP-1 medications might influence the brain. Their potential cognitive effects could result from improvements in metabolic health, direct actions within the brain, or a combination of both.

Understanding these mechanisms could help researchers identify which patients are most likely to benefit and potentially lead to medications designed specifically to support memory and other thinking abilities.

Christoffer Clemmensen, the review's senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity treatments to explore the connection between metabolism and the brain.

"Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function," says Christoffer Clemmensen.

The researchers are calling for clinical trials that evaluate memory, attention, and other cognitive abilities beginning when patients first start treatment. Following these changes over time could help establish whether GLP-1 drugs genuinely protect brain function and clarify who might benefit most.

They also stress that treatment is not without potential drawbacks, particularly for older adults and people who are physically frail. Rapid weight loss can lead to a reduction in muscle mass, which may weaken physical function and offset some of the possible benefits.

Careful monitoring will therefore be essential as researchers investigate whether today's weight loss and diabetes medications could eventually provide new ways to protect the brain.

#4286. Limbus Company tier list - The best Identities for each character

We will be going over the best Identities for each character and what makes them so strong, explaining through the whole Limbus Company tier list.

Updated on November 17th, 2026 - Version: 1.119.0 - Added: [Haute Couture:: Le Noir 3F Public Adress Room] Hong Lu, [The Sword Sharpened with Tears] Hong Lu, [Wedge Office Fixer] Sinclair, [Wedge Office Fixer] Don Quixote, [Wedge Office Rep] Outis

In the Limbus Company tier list below, we have compared each Identity and ranked them according to their overall power and usefulness.

But first, a word on rerolling. Given the length of the tutorial section being rather large and every Identity you can get from the first roll you make on the gacha banner, it's my own opinion that re-rolling is basically worthless here. Still, if you're truly after a specific Identity, you can do so simply by resetting your account in the game options once they're accessible.

With that out of the way, click on the blue button below and let's check out our Limbus Company tier list together!

The best Identities at the moment are sorted and ranked at the top of our Limbus Company tier list, as usual. If you have them, you're set - if you don't, try to acquire them when they have a Rate Up banner. Although many Identities are very good in the game overall, these deserve a tier of their own.

Heathcliff - R Corp. 4th Pack Rabbit Despite not having any way to refresh his Ammo Count, this version of Heathcliff inflicts lots of Bleed, Fragile, and Rupture, which are all hyper-damaging debuffs to whichever target. Throw in his massively damaging abilities, and he’s a force to be reckoned with.

Sinclair - The One Who Shall Grip Sinclair's newest Identity goes hand-in-hand with The One Who Grips, as their passives bounce off one another to do lots of damage. Much like his predecessor, he does lots of Bleed damage and focuses on purely Blunt skills. Add in the ability to raise his own Stagger Threshold, and this new version of Sinclair seems to dominate pretty strongly.

Hong Lu - Tingtang Gang Leader Tingtang Gang Leader revolves around re-casting two of the three abilities specific to this Identity, one re-casting if the opponent has less than 25% HP, and the other fully choosing a new target if you kill the first target with it. Specifically, you should focus on using Mutilate as much as possible on low HP targets to then re-cast it over and over on the squishier opponents.

Ishmael - LCCB Assistant Manager Another Ammo-based character, which is probably the only pitfall of this Identity. LCCB Ishamel is pretty good at winning clashes, though she could be better. But she is one of the few who can apply Rupture and Tremor to opponents, buffing up your team's damage significantly. The other downfall of this Identity is that all of her abilities are Blunt, so be sure to know the enemy's resistance before you add her to your roster.

Faust - The One Who Grips The One Who Grips is, despite a nerf or two, an incredibly strong Identity. This Identity makes Faust the main villain of chapter 3 of the story mode, and brings with it some incredibly powerful abilities. Two out of three of her abilities utilise pierce damage, and the last does blunt, so don’t expect her to have a place on your slash team. All of these abilities hit really hard, though, and apply lots of bleed, so she's basically a mainstay in just about any composition.

Hong Lu - Kurokumo Clan Wakashu You may see this Identity ranking quite well in our Limbus Company tier lists and think that a 2-star wouldn’t match up to Hong Lu’s 3-star variant. What you don’t know, however, is that this 2-star rarity Identity is one of the best in the game. Oriented around slash attacks, Kurokumo Hong Lu specifically has the ability Cloud Cutter, which deals up to six Bleed to an enemy who has no current Bleed stacks. This is possibly the strongest ability in the entire game, so be sure not to sleep on this Identity.

Outis - Seven Association South Section 6 Director This version of Outis is easily her best due to her Passive ability, which deals extra damage if you are doing damage that the target is Weak or Fatal to, and each ability of hers debuffing the target’s offence and defence, respectively. If you are facing a boss, Seven Section 6 Outis is great to use to debuff them down to an easier level. Still, she has her flaws, so she can't move past the middle of this tier list at the moment.

Ryoshu - Kurokumo Clan Wakashu This 3-star version of Ryoshu is powerful for the same reason as the Kurokumo version of Hong Lu, which is her ability to put huge stacks of Bleed on an opponent, as well as debuff them and do more damage depending on the stacks of Bleed the target has. Combine her with the Kurokumo version of Hong Lu, and you won't struggle with any current content.

Gregor - G Corp. Manager Corporal Gregor's only 3-star variant thus far focuses on self-sustaining, with each ability healing him for a set amount. This makes him a tough one to beat on the field, though he does fall a little short, given that his abilities aren't super strong in Clashes outside of Dismember. Still, he’s a worthy addition to any team composition.

Ryoshu - R.B. Chef de Cuisine Another big Bleed stacker, this version of Ryoshu can deal hefty damage with both her Bleed abilities and the fact that I Can Cook Anything does way more damage if the target has low HP. Add in her Passives, which heal the lowest HP ally on your team when an enemy is defeated, and she’s a solid pick for long Dungeons specifically.

Meursault - N Corp. Groẞhammer Groẞhammer is another N Corp Identity, much like The One Who Grips, and utilises the same two-pierce, one blunt set-up. Once again, this one does lots of Bleed, but also holds the ability to heal himself on any hit with Annihilate Heretics, too. He’s basically strong for the same reasons The One Who Grips is, but with some self-healing added in too.

Beyond the top of this tier list, the remainder of the characters are all decent options in one way or another, but most require more investment than the ones above to stand out. Some notable exceptions are Don Quixote’s W Corp. Cleanup Agent Identity, which can dish out huge damage but is kept back by not being able to keep her Charge count up. Alongside her, I’d point out that Faust’s Lobotomy Corp Remnant Identity is a pretty strong Clasher, but falls short in most other departments when compared to stronger slash-based Identities.

Otherwise, Identities beyond the ones mentioned above aren’t worthless by any stretch of the imagination because they are outclassed by their stronger variants. Focus on grabbing those in the S Tier, and you will be able to tackle all of the current content in Limbus Company with ease!

There are other similar lists that you can take a look at, like our Legend Clover tier list, or this Call of Dragons tier list, to name a few. Of course, we have a lot more, so take a look around!

#4285. 10 Party Members I Benched Immediately (and Still Feel Guilty About)

Contributor at DualShockers, former Esports Insider DACH content lead, former Escapist Magazine Germany content lead, software engineering background.

I have a complicated relationship with the party menu. In any RPG with more companions than party slots, somebody has to stay behind at camp, and whilst I would love to tell you that I rotate everyone fairly, that would be a lie. Some characters get benched within minutes of joining, and most of them never make it back out.

Whether it's through mid-battle character switching or something a little more esoteric, these JRPGs all make you rethink your party mid-battle!

It is rarely personal. Some of them are too slow, some arrive too late, and some simply have the misfortune of standing next to a character I like more. I do still feel guilty about every single one of them, though, so let’s take a look at ten party members I benched immediately, and why I’m still a little bit sorry about it.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is a very interesting case when it comes to companions: a lot of them start out really, really unlikable. Then you get to know them and their motivations, and it suddenly becomes quite understandable why they act the way that they do. Larian Studios did that so well that benching anyone feels a little bit like abandoning a friend.

Gale is the one I leave at camp regardless. I don’t mind his storyline at all, but I simply don’t enjoy the way wizards work, with every spell slot spent bringing you one step closer to yet another long rest. I usually play a Warlock myself, and having a reliable cantrip like Eldritch Blast means that I never have to worry about that kind of balancing act, especially early on.

It also doesn’t help that there are plenty of companions I like a lot more. Gale’s personality is just a bit goofy for my taste, and whilst I did keep him around for one full playthrough to properly get to know him and his story, I have never felt the need to repeat that. He is a perfectly lovely man. He’s just a perfectly lovely man who waits at camp.

Blue mages have always been one of the more interesting concepts in Final Fantasy. Their magic tends to be really powerful, since there has to be a reason to use them over your regular black, white and even red mages, and that usually means they go from being a bit weak to being suddenly wildly overpowered. Kimahri should be exactly that kind of character.

The problem is that his blue magic is tied to his Overdrive. He learns enemy abilities with Lancet, but can only use them as his Ronso Rage, and whilst there are ways to charge Overdrives faster later on, it makes him awkward for a large part of the game. Everyone else in the party already has a clearly defined role, too, and Kimahri sits in his own odd little corner of the Sphere Grid without one.

Now, I tend to 100% every Final Fantasy, so he does get used eventually. If I’m simply building a party, though, he is the last character on my mind, which is a shame. Truth be told, the story doesn’t help, either: as Yuna’s guardian, he barely speaks early on, and that makes it hard to form an emotional connection with him. His character design is absolutely sick, mind you.

Sharla is a trap, and I say that with love. When she first joins in Xenoblade Chronicles, she is a pretty good character: a dedicated healer with some decent ether arts, at a point where you have nobody else to bench her for. That is precisely where the problem starts.

Because she feels essential early on, you keep her, even as better options join. She deals next to no damage, though, which means that fights take longer, and longer fights mean that you take more damage. All of that damage then gets healed by Sharla, who ends up looking far more useful than she actually is.

I fell for it on my first playthrough, and I have seen plenty of others do exactly the same. A dedicated healer just isn’t all that necessary once you double down on damage or find more flexible healing elsewhere, like Shulk’s Light Heal. Sharla has been on my bench ever since, and I do feel bad about it, since none of this is really her fault.

From controversial clowns to big blue lionmen, Final Fantasy has party members you remember for being utterly useless but who are anything but!

For the longest time, I was shackled by what party composition makes sense for the story, and I still struggle with letting go of that sometimes. You will never catch me playing a Pokémon game without my starter, for example. In a similar vein, many of my Tales of Symphonia playthroughs simply ended up with Lloyd, Colette, Raine and Genis, because they are the ones who have known each other from the very beginning.

Eventually, I managed to get over myself. Since then, without fail, Genis has never been in my party again. I like the conversations between him and Lloyd, and I do believe that pairing a carefree character with a snarkier, more considerate one works out really well.

I just usually find him a bit grating. That is a harsh thing to say about a child who has been through as much as Genis has, and I’m aware of that every time I move him out of the party. It hasn’t stopped me yet.

Kongol always ends up benched. It’s common knowledge that Rose falls off quite aggressively on Disc 2, and again on Disc 4, which is unfortunate, but even she has seen more action in my playthroughs than he has. For the last surviving Giganto, that has to sting.

My issue is simple: I don’t usually enjoy very slow characters, and Kongol is incredibly strong but painfully slow. To make him properly useful, you have to boost both his speed and his magic defence quite aggressively, and I would rather spend that effort on someone who doesn’t need it. He never stood much of a chance with me.

Luckily, The Legend of Dragoon isn’t a particularly hard game at the best of times, so you can beat it with any party you like. That takes some of the guilt away. Kongol saved Dart and his friends from a falling pillar before joining them, though, and I repaid him with the better part of four discs spent sitting around.

It pains me so much to say this, because I love dogs! In Dragon Age: Origins, however, Dog is close to useless compared to anyone else. Unless you install a mod, he takes up a full party slot, just like any other companion would, and he can’t carry a fight the way they can.

He does a semi-decent job in the first few levels, since Alistair and Sten aren’t great tanks at that stage, either. He then gets outscaled quickly, as your warriors pick up their defensive talents and proper tank gear, and on Nightmare difficulty, that gap becomes very hard to ignore. Dog isn’t beefy enough to be a tank and doesn’t deal enough damage to make up for it, which leaves him without a clear role.

His Overwhelm ability is devastating against a single dangerous target, mages in particular, but that is about it. It’s a real shame, because his interactions with the other companions are often hilarious. Leaving him at camp means missing out on those, and it never gets any easier.

What is interesting, though, is that there exists a Extra Dog Slot mod that lets him tag along as a fifth party member, and it shows up on nearly every list of essential mods for the game. I am clearly not the only one with a guilty conscience.

Goofy has done nothing wrong, and I want that on record. My problem with the first Kingdom Hearts is that nearly every world offers a guest character who can take Donald’s or Goofy’s place, and I love how unique that makes each world feel. Somebody has to make room, and it was usually Goofy.

Recently, I felt really bad about that, and I wanted to make it right in my latest playthrough. Sadly, all it did was make me realise that the guest characters are a big part of the game’s charm for me. Fighting alongside Ariel or the Beast is simply too cool to pass up, and since they can’t leave their home worlds, it always feels like now or never.

So Goofy might have to sit this one out a little longer. He will take it well, because he is Goofy. That only makes it worse.

With a single action or word, there are moments in these Nintendo DS JRPGs Where Companions Can Derail the Entire Story.

Jean is the most painful example of wasted potential I can think of. His design is memorable, his personality is fun, and being the frog prince of SimaFort sets him apart from everyone else in Breath of Fire II. He believes that there are no bad people in the world, only bad hearts, and he says all of it in a faux-French accent.

Mechanically, sadly, he has very little to offer. He joins slow and underwhelming, with good defence but incredibly low agility, and his stats never match the way he looks. His Holy fusion turns him into a tall, heroic-looking frog knight who can in theory become quite formidable, but it comes too late and with too many trade-offs to justify his slot over characters who have already proven themselves.

Jean isn’t unplayable. He is a “what could have been”: a character who looks like he should be iconic in battle, but never gets the chance to live up to it. If he had been a little more like Frog in Chrono Trigger, with some healing to offer, he might have been worthwhile well before the endgame.

Yangus is easily one of the most lovable characters in Dragon Quest VIII, and I still barely use him for long stretches of the game. He is the dedicated tank, and the job gradually overwhelms him: magic can lower his armour, most of his equipment reduces his evasion, and he is very slow. He has a respectable Strength base, but not much gets built on top of it.

In the 3DS version, which added Red and Morrie as party members, that makes him the obvious candidate for the sidelines once the new recruits join. He can become useful again in the late game, but that means building his Scythe tree from the ground up. That is a lot to ask for a character I have already replaced.

It isn’t all doom and gloom, since he simply dips in the mid-game. Early on, 16 skill points in Humanity get you Nose for Treasure, which tells you how many chests are left in an area, and that is quite useful. I just wish that was enough to keep him in the party.

Nino joins with such a good story that you really want to use her and help her grow. Raised by the Black Fang, she is sent to assassinate Prince Zephiel in Battle Before Dawn, has a change of heart and ends up fleeing with Jaffar instead. By the time she joins you, it’s impossible not to root for her.

Unfortunately, she arrives as a Level 5 Mage very late in the game, when you are most likely fielding promoted units. Her growth rates are amongst the highest in the game, so she will catch up if you put the time in, but she’s a glass cannon until then, and there isn’t much game left. Unless you wrap your whole strategy around her, she gets benched immediately. This makes her a classic example of what Fire Emblem fans call the Est archetype: a unit that joins late and underlevelled, but with enormous potential.

Sometimes, it feels like her sole purpose is to stand between you and recruiting Jaffar, since he only joins if she talks to him and they both survive. This tiny mage is brimming with potential, and I have made use of it in some playthroughs. I’m just not always in the mood for that, so more often than not, she ends up on the bench.

Crisp air, hot coffee and a cozy sofa: autumn is when I reach for nostalgia, and these ten GameCube JRPGs still make the trip back worthwhile.

#4284. This remarkable new material could solve a major carbon capture problem

A newly developed material from Oregon State University could help solve one of the biggest challenges in industrial carbon capture: removing carbon dioxide from emissions that contain large amounts of water vapor. Instead of allowing moisture to interfere with the process, the material uses it to help maintain effective carbon capture.

The researchers have filed a patent application for the innovation, which belongs to a class of materials known as metal-organic frameworks, or MOFs. Their findings, published in Angewandte Chemie, could help make carbon capture more practical and affordable for factories and other industrial facilities.

The advance could have important implications for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Industrial operations, including the burning of fossil fuels to produce energy, are major sources of atmospheric carbon dioxide. In the United States, industry accounts for 30% of total greenhouse gas emissions, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.

A New Material That Overcomes a Major Carbon Capture Problem

The new material, called BVR-X, has an unusual internal structure that keeps water and carbon dioxide largely separated within its microscopic pores. By directing the two substances into different regions, it prevents water molecules from occupying the spaces needed to capture carbon dioxide.

"This internal organization helps the material work under conditions that more closely resemble real industrial emissions," said Kyriakos Stylianou, professor of chemistry in the OSU College of Science.

MOFs are crystalline materials built from positively charged metal ions connected by organic molecules called ligands, which act as linkers. The metal ions form connection points, or nodes, while the linkers join them together into repeating structures resembling tiny cages. These structures contain extremely small pores that can trap gas molecules on their internal surfaces through a process called adsorption, much like a sponge holds substances within its structure.

One of the advantages of MOFs is their remarkable adaptability. Scientists can combine different metals and organic linkers to create materials with specific characteristics. According to Stylianou, millions of MOF designs are theoretically possible. Researchers have already synthesized more than 100,000 distinct MOFs and predicted the properties of hundreds of thousands more.

Why Carbon Capture Needs Better Materials

"The capture of CO2 is critical for meeting net-zero emission targets," said Stylianou, who directs OSU's Materials Discovery Laboratory, known as the MaD Lab. "MOFs have shown a lot of promise because of their porosity and their structural versatility."

Carbon dioxide is a major greenhouse gas released when fossil fuels are burned. As it accumulates in the atmosphere, it traps heat and contributes to global warming.

One approach to addressing the problem involves removing carbon dioxide directly from the atmosphere. Facilities designed for this purpose are beginning to operate in different parts of the world. The world's largest such plant opened in Iceland in 2024, although its annual carbon removal capacity is still relatively small compared with global emissions. According to Stylianou, the facility can capture roughly as much carbon dioxide in one year as about 7,200 cars produce over the same period.

Capturing carbon dioxide before it reaches the atmosphere is another option, and the technologies used for this purpose are considerably more established. At factories and power plants, carbon capture systems can intercept emissions as they travel through exhaust systems and smokestacks. Some of these systems use MOFs to adsorb carbon dioxide molecules from the passing gases.

How Water Makes Industrial Carbon Capture Difficult

A major obstacle, however, is that industrial exhaust often contains substantial amounts of water vapor. Many MOFs that perform well in controlled laboratory experiments lose much of their carbon capture ability when exposed to the humid conditions found in actual smokestacks.

The gases can be dried before carbon dioxide is removed, but doing so requires additional equipment and energy. Those costs can become so significant that the overall process is no longer economically practical for industrial use.

BVR-X offers a different approach. Rather than requiring moisture to be removed, the material responds to water in a way that preserves its ability to collect carbon dioxide. Its internal organization allows water and carbon dioxide to occupy different regions, helping prevent the competition that normally undermines carbon capture performance.

"Water usually makes capturing carbon dioxide more difficult," he said. "Our new material does something unusual: It responds to water by changing in a way that lets it keep capturing CO2 effectively even under very humid conditions."

Strong Performance Under Realistic Industrial Conditions

Laboratory tests demonstrated that BVR-X could efficiently capture carbon dioxide from a highly humid gas stream containing only 4% carbon dioxide.

That concentration is particularly relevant to emissions from burning natural gas, where carbon dioxide makes up a relatively small proportion of the exhaust. Extracting it becomes especially difficult when large quantities of water vapor are also present.

The experiments therefore tested the material under conditions that resemble an important real-world challenge, "where separating a small amount of CO2 in the presence of substantial water is particularly challenging," said Stylianou.

The researchers also found that BVR-X could repeatedly capture and release carbon dioxide without losing its effectiveness over dozens of cycles. This ability to regenerate the material is important because commercial carbon capture systems must reuse their capture materials many times to keep operating costs manageable.

"And the material can be regenerated and reused, maintaining performance through dozens of capture-and-release cycles and tolerating demanding conditions," he added. "Those are important qualities for practical carbon-capture technologies."

The results suggest that BVR-X could help overcome a major limitation of existing MOF technologies, particularly in industrial settings where removing moisture from exhaust gases would otherwise be costly.

The study brought together researchers from several institutions. Stylianou worked with MaD Lab members Ankit Yadav, Emmanuel Musa and Andrzej Gładysiak, along with Micah Hickethier, Chun-Wai Chang and Kai Shen Choong from the Oregon State College of Engineering.

Additional collaborators included scientists from the University of California, Berkeley; the University of Oregon; and the ARAMCO Research and Development Center.

Funding was provided by Saudi Aramco, the Murdock Charitable Trust, and a donor-advised fund established by Oregon State University alumni and retired public school teachers Brian and Marilyn Kleiner through the OSU Foundation.

Against world No.1 FURIA on Wednesday, The MongolZ recovered after dropping the opening map. MOUZ have also booked a semi-final place after going unbeaten in Group B.

The defeat ended a seven-game winning run for FURIA, HLTV said, although the match was not an elimination game. FURIA had not lost since winning PGL Masters Bucharest. They now face BetBoom in the quarter-finals.

The second map, Cache, was FURIA’s own pick, and The MongolZ had lost on that map in each of their previous four attempts. This time they won it, then closed out the series on the third map.

Falcons went out in the Group A lower-bracket final. NAVI recovered from a narrow loss on the opening map and dominated the rest of the series. On the Mirage decider, NAVI won all 12 rounds of their T-side half.

w0nderful went 25-4 on Inferno. b1t then took over on Mirage.

#4281. Arc Raiders just keeps breaking its own Steam player records

Word of mouth has done wonders for the popularity of Arc Raiders, clearly more than all the pre-launch marketing and hype.

Arc Raiders just cannot be stopped. The extraction shooter from Embark Studios has once again attracted more players over the weekend than it has in its launch week, and over its first weekend on the market.

The positive reception the PvPvE game has garnered from players has clearly caused many of them to convince their friends to jump into this unique gem of a game.

The day Arc Raiders launched, it peaked at 264,673 concurrent players on Steam. Although not massive, it was quite a bit more than the game’s most popular - free - beta test managed to attract.

That figure was broken yet again over the game’s first weekend, with Arc Raiders having reached 354,836 concurrent players on Steam. This is where many thought it would settle, as we start to see the gradual - and expected - decline of player numbers.

To everyone’s surprise, however, Arc Raiders shattered even that record yet again on Sunday, November 9. According to SteamDB, the game peaked at 462,488 concurrent players on Steam, which is a sizeable increase on its launch day numbers. Indeed, should this trend continue, Arc Raiders is going to be well on its way to doubling its initial launch record.

While a few games have broken their launch Steam player records in the past, it’s incredibly rare to see it happen - especially twice in such a short period after launch. Embark clearly has a winner on its hands here.

Arc Raiders’ next big moment is the game’s first post-launch map, which is set to arrive at some point this month, alongside new Quests and other gameplay items. Seeing as how the Steam concurrent record has been broken twice, there’s every chance the arrival of the new map will bring another boost to player numbers.

If you’re among the millions of players who have been exploring the Rust Belt, you’re probably wondering where to find prickly pears, where to find lemons and apricots, and where to find olives - and those links will answer all of those questions. And, if you just jumped in over the weekend, you’re definitely going to find these Arc Raiders tips very helpful.

#4278. Battlefield 6 patch finally ends the menace of the Lock-Guided Missile, shuts down the Recon Drone Sledgehammer exploit and more

Today's Battlefield 6 patch is laser-focused on taking care of some of the more infuriating bugs while also taking out a couple of exploits.

The next Battlefield 6 update is here. Having gone live just moments ago, update 1.1.1.5 is something of a midseason update, bringing a few quality of life tweaks to the game alongside some key fixes for a few of the issues that cropped up since the launch of Season 1 in late October.

This latest release is also the first to tackle some of the problems players have been running into playing Redsec battle royale, the free-to-play component that also came out recently.

Patch 1.1.1.5 is fairly limited in scope. The biggest fix in this one comes to the Lock-Guided Missiles going through flares, and generally being annoying enough to stop players from using air vehicles altogether.

The Lock-Guided Missiles were mainly used by AA vehicles, but they could also be equipped by IFVs, which made it even more of a nightmare to pilots. It got so bad that Battlefield Studios disabled it entirely while the team worked on a proper fix.

Another exploit the patch fixes is the one that allowed players to stand on the Recon Drone and reach areas they’re not supposed to. This was done by… repeatedly hitting it with a Sledgehammer. The long-running issue of vehicles not spawning for certain teams in Conquest and Breakthrough appears to have finally been fixed, too.

In terms of battle royale, the patch has a few fixes that should help make the experience more consistent, as well as improve the flow of matches. One of the more interesting addresses an issue that could eliminate the entire squad instead of reviving dead teammates when using a Mobile Spawn.

Patch 1.1.1.5 also has yet more adjustments to weapon dispersion (bloom). Some of the casses it addresses include transitioning from sprint to firing in ADS, and others where it apparently scaled with player movement speed.

While the 2025 reveal of the Switch 2 came with many surprises, none were as unexpected as The Duskbloods. It's a Switch 2 exclusive, multiplayer-only title from FromSoftware, the developer behind games like Dark Souls and Elden Ring; in other words, not your typical Nintendo game. While The Duskbloods was originally scheduled to launch sometime this year, today the developer announced it's pushing the game's launch to 2027.

According to a post on The Duskbloods' X account, the main reason for the delay was balance-related. Here's the full statement:

While development of "The Duskbloods" is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027. We apologize to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support. During the network test, we saw active interest in the core concepts of the game, including combat, strategic depth, and player expression. To further enhance these aspects, we have decided to move the launch, allowing time for final adjustments to game rules and balancing.

We attended a hands-on preview session earlier this year and came away very positive, and sentiment was similar following the game's closed network test (that is, when the servers were working properly). It's not surprising that the devs have changes in mind following so much public feedback, though it is a little surprising that it will take until sometime next year for those adjustments to be complete.

#4275. Arc Raiders has proven that extraction shooters can be popular, with over 4 million copies sold in under two weeks

Arc Raiders has sold even more copies, which we should've guessed, given that the game keeps breaking its own concurrent player records.

It’s pretty clear at this stage that Arc Raiders is one of the biggest launches of 2025. More interesting than the numbers themselves, however, is that this is an extraction shooter - a subgenre which has typically been thought of as niche.

If you’ve been paying the PvPvE game any attention, you could easily see how (and why) it keeps breaking its own records.

Today, publisher Nexon announced in a press release (via Gematsu) that Arc Raiders has now sold over 4 million copies. The game came out on October 30, which means it managed to sell that many copies in a little over 10 days.

The news comes on the same day that developer Embark Studios announced that the game had more than 700,000 concurrent players across all platforms over the weekend. Over the same weekend on Steam alone, Arc Raiders broke its own Steam concurrent record with a new peak of 462,488 players - which is a significant chunk of that 700,000+ player base.

This marks the second time the extraction shooter has broken its own concurrent player records, which is something very few games have managed in the past. Arc Raiders remains a top-seller, too. On Steam, it’s currently the second-best seller globally (by revenue), sitting just below Counter-Strike 2.

“The many different ways you play and participate in ARC Raiders have completely blown us away, going far beyond what we ever imagined. You surprise us, you outsmart us, and you keep us on our toes. We wouldn’t have it any other way,” the developer wrote on Twitter.

Embark recently published a roadmap to highlight all the new content coming to the game over the remainder of this year. The first new map is set to arrive this month alongside new Arc units, new gameplay items, new events and more.

Just over the weekend, the game received several new Map Conditions that completely alter the way they play. The developer has already rolled out a couple of updates since launch, in order to tackle exploits and fix a few launchday bugs.

If you’re currently hooked on this gem of a game, we guarantee that our Arc Raiders gameplay tips will have at least one you didn’t know about. We also have more guides on how to find some of the more elusive items in the game, such as olives, lemons and apricots, and prickly pears.

#4272. 8 Soulslikes With Insane Difficulty Spikes

Christian Bognar is a Contributor at DualShockers with over three years of experience covering the gaming industry. Since 2022, he has written guides and reviews for publications including DualShockers, CBR, Attack of the Fanboy, PC Invasion, and The Game Slayer. He holds a Bachelor’s Degree in Business Administration

The Soulslikes genre offers some of the greatest challenges in gaming. With difficult bosses, enemies that demand patience, and many obstacles throughout a level, meeting success in any Soulslike can be incredibly rewarding.

However, there are times when a game takes it too far and includes a harsh difficulty spike that seemingly comes out of nowhere. This could sometimes lead to areas of the game feeling a bit unfair.

It's not the genre's area of expertise, but some of its representatives are more daring, offering fascinating movement mechanics.

While the games listed in this article are some of the best entries in the genre, they do have pacing issues when it comes to difficulty. Here are eight Soulslikes with brutal difficulty spikes.

Sekiro is already a demanding game from the get-go, but its difficulty reaches a whole other level in the mid to late game. Enemies become more aggressive, minibosses hit harder, and all encounters will constantly remind players that they need to master the parry system to stand a chance.

Boss fights also become considerably more demanding, requiring players to learn lengthy attack patterns and maintain constant pressure rather than relying on dodging. Just when you thought you were getting good at the game, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice raises the bar.

The expansion of Elden Ring, Shadow of the Erdtree, is known for its difficulty spike right from the start. As soon as you enter the Land of Shadow, you’ll realize enemies deal way more damage, and your character is much weaker overall.

With the introduction of Scadutree Fragments, items that raise attack power and defense, players essentially have to start from scratch and engage with a new progression system. In other words, even OP base-game builds get a wake-up call when starting the DLC.

Overall, Lies of P is generally on the easier side for a Soulslike. However, the game has brutal difficulty spikes in a handful of its bosses. For example, Laxasia the Complete, Simon Manus, and King of Puppets are ten times more challenging than anything else in the game.

Each of these bosses is a true test of reflexes and endurance, where even the smallest mistake can prove costly. What makes these encounters particularly jarring is the stark contrast in difficulty, as the areas leading up to them are relatively easy to breeze through.

There’s no denying that The First Berserker: Khazan is a very challenging game right from its first level. Still, despite it being a very tough experience through and through, it still features an insane difficulty spike in its second half that can sometimes feel pretty unfair.

Late-game bosses are some of the most demanding encounters the genre has to offer, featuring relentless combos that leave very little room for mistakes. Khazan’s combat is super satisfying, but players who haven’t mastered its mechanics will quickly discover just how unforgiving it can be.

If you're looking for the heir to Soulsborne games, look no further than this list of ten Soulslikes that are unexpected masterpieces.

While the 2023 version of Lords of the Fallen never reaches the difficulty heights of 2014’s, it’s definitely not an easy experience. The game reaches its peak in difficulty during Bramis Castle, an area filled with the hardest enemies in the entire game.

Bramis Castle has been heavily regarded as unfair by many players due to the absurd amount of elite enemies. It was so hard that there were multiple post-launch patches to make it feel more reasonable. Still, despite the patches to make it easier, Bramis Castle remains an insane difficulty spike.

The original Hollow Knight was a fairly well-balanced experience from beginning to end, and while Silksong is a phenomenal game, it’s not as consistent as the original. For example, Bilewater increases the difficulty tenfold due to poisonous waters and brutal platforming.

Additionally, Act 3 of Silksong introduces an entirely new set of challenges as the Void corrupts Pharloom, making enemies considerably more dangerous while changing areas and levels. Fortunately, Act 3 is completely optional, meaning players who aren’t interested in tackling this difficulty spike can simply ignore it.

Wuchang: Fallen Feathers features several notoriously sharp difficulty spikes, mainly in its boss fights. Wuchang has the tendency to make the player feel incredibly powerful while exploring a level and then completely ripping that feeling away during some of the main bosses.

One of the earliest examples of this is the Commander Honglan boss fight, the first brick wall players will hit in a playthrough. All earlier bosses are a walk in the park compared to Commander Honglan, and everything that follows involves bosses that demand fast reflexes and perfect performance.

Nioh 3's difficulty spikes can be particularly unforgiving, especially when players enter the Heian Period. This period involves some of the most challenging locations and bosses in the game, such as Ibaraki Doji, Kajiwara Kagetoki, and many more.

Pretty much, once the player enters the Heian Period, the real Nioh 3 experience begins, and the rest of the adventure is a true test of skill. Bosses hit hard, are faster, and the importance of leveling equipment increases dramatically.

There's nothing more fitting for this season than being destroyed by the same boss fifty-seven times in a row.
